body:
Why biotechnology requires safeguards

Biotechnology uses living organisms, cells, enzymes or biological materials to develop useful products and processes. Traditional applications include making curd and producing medicines through microorganisms. Modern biotechnology also includes recombinant DNA technology, genetic modification, genome sequencing and gene-based medical research.

These advances can improve agriculture, healthcare and environmental management. However, their benefits do not eliminate the need to examine possible risks. A microorganism may cause accidental infection, a genetically modified crop may interact with organisms in its surroundings, and a person's genetic information may reveal sensitive details about health and family relationships.

Three related fields address these concerns: biosafety, bioethics and biosecurity. They overlap, but each addresses a different central question.

The 3 fundamental concepts

Biosafety

Biosafety means the principles, practices and safeguards used to prevent unintended exposure to biological hazards or their accidental release into the environment.

Biosafety protects laboratory workers, research participants where applicable, surrounding communities, animals, plants and ecosystems. It includes assessing risks before activities begin, selecting suitable containment measures, following safe handling practices and preventing unintended environmental release.

For example, before a genetically engineered crop is released into the environment, its possible effects on other organisms and the surrounding ecosystem must be assessed. The purpose is to establish whether the proposed activity can proceed under appropriate safety conditions.

Bioethics

Bioethics examines the moral principles that guide decisions involving living organisms, medicine, biological research and biotechnology.

Bioethics asks whether an activity respects people's rights, protects their welfare, distributes benefits and burdens fairly, and treats affected individuals and communities responsibly.

For example, a genetic study may be scientifically useful and physically safe but still be unethical if researchers collect identifiable genetic information without valid consent or disclose sensitive findings without appropriate authorization.

Biosecurity

Biosecurity, in the context of biotechnology, means measures intended to prevent the unauthorized access, loss, theft, diversion or deliberate misuse of biological materials, related technology and sensitive biological information.

Biosecurity addresses deliberate misuse and failures of control that could enable misuse. It includes appropriate access restrictions, accountability for sensitive biological materials, institutional oversight and responsible handling of information.

For example, an institution may restrict access to certain biological materials and sensitive research records so that they cannot be obtained or used without authorization.

Comparison of the 3 safeguards

AspectBiosafetyBioethicsBiosecurity
Main concernUnintended biological harmRight and wrong conductUnauthorized access and deliberate misuse
Central questionCan accidental harm be prevented?Is the activity ethically justified?Can misuse be prevented?
Typical measuresRisk assessment and containmentConsent and independent ethical reviewAccess control and accountability
ExamplePreventing accidental escape of a modified organismObtaining consent for genetic researchPreventing unauthorized removal of biological material

How the safeguards work together

Consider a research project investigating a genetically modified crop. Biosafety examines possible effects on workers, other organisms and the environment. Bioethics considers whether the expected benefits justify the burdens and whether affected people are treated fairly. Biosecurity addresses unauthorized access to sensitive materials or information.

If the same project also collects genetic samples from human participants, informed consent, confidentiality and ethical review become additional requirements. If it uses biological resources or associated traditional knowledge from a community, access and benefit-sharing obligations may also arise.

Genetically modified organisms and living modified organisms

A genetically modified organism (GMO) is an organism whose genetic material has been altered through genetic engineering or related biotechnology techniques. A living modified organism (LMO), as defined by the Cartagena Protocol, is a living organism possessing a novel combination of genetic material obtained through modern biotechnology.

The term LMO emphasizes that the organism is alive and capable of transferring or replicating genetic material. A viable genetically engineered seed may qualify as an LMO. A highly processed product derived from a genetically modified organism is not necessarily an LMO because it may contain no living modified organism.

This distinction matters because international biosafety rules governing the movement of LMOs do not automatically apply in the same way to every processed product derived from genetic modification.

Scientific safety and ethical acceptability are different judgments. Demonstrating that an activity presents an acceptable biological risk does not automatically establish that consent, fairness, privacy or access requirements have been satisfied.

Prelims focus

  • Biosafety primarily addresses accidental exposure and unintended release.
  • Bioethics addresses consent, rights, welfare, justice and responsible conduct.
  • Biosecurity addresses unauthorized access, diversion and deliberate misuse.
  • LMO means living modified organism; GMO means genetically modified organism.
  • Trap: Biosafety and biosecurity overlap, but preventing accidental exposure is not identical to preventing intentional misuse.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class XII, Chapter 11, Biotechnology: Principles and Processes, Section 11.1; Chapter 12, Biotechnology and its Applications, Section 12.4; World Health Organization, Laboratory Biosafety Manual, 4th edition, 2020, Overview; World Health Organization, Global Guidance Framework for the Responsible Use of the Life Sciences, 2022, Overview; Convention on Biological Diversity, Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, Article 3. Online sources consulted 13 November 2026.]

title: Biosafety, Bioethics and Biosecurity: Meaning and Fundamental Differences

body:
What is biological risk assessment?

Biological risk assessment is the systematic identification and evaluation of possible harmful effects associated with a biological activity, material or organism. It helps decision-makers determine whether an activity is acceptable and what precautions or restrictions are necessary.

Risk assessment is important in laboratories, agricultural biotechnology, biological research and activities involving genetically engineered organisms. It is especially relevant before a living modified organism is introduced into an environment where it may survive, reproduce or interact with other organisms.

Hazard and risk are not the same

A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm. A risk concerns the likelihood and consequences of that harm under particular conditions.

For example, a microorganism may have the ability to cause disease. This is a hazardous characteristic. The actual risk to a person depends on factors such as whether exposure can occur, the nature of the activity, the person's susceptibility and the safeguards already in place.

Hazard describes the potential for harm; risk considers the possibility and seriousness of harm in a particular situation. The presence of a hazard does not establish that harmful exposure will certainly occur.

Important factors in risk assessment

Nature of the biological agent or organism

Assessors examine relevant biological properties, including whether an organism can cause disease, survive in a particular environment, reproduce or interact with other organisms. For a genetically modified organism, the introduced characteristic and any relevant changes in its behaviour are considered.

Possible exposure

Risk depends partly on who or what might come into contact with the hazard. Possible recipients include laboratory personnel, animals, plants, consumers, soil organisms and surrounding ecosystems.

Exposure may be unlikely under effective containment but become more relevant if a living organism is deliberately released into an open environment.

Severity and likelihood of harm

Assessors consider how serious a possible adverse effect could be and the likelihood of its occurrence. They also examine the reliability of the available evidence and any important uncertainties.

Comparison with appropriate alternatives

A scientifically meaningful evaluation considers a suitable comparison, such as a genetically modified crop and its non-modified parent under comparable environmental conditions. This helps identify effects associated with the modification rather than effects already present in the ordinary crop.

Basic sequence of risk assessment

  1. Identify possible hazards: Determine what adverse effects could occur.
  2. Identify possible exposure: Determine which people, organisms or environments might be affected and under what conditions.
  3. Evaluate likelihood and consequences: Examine scientific evidence about the probability and seriousness of each relevant effect.
  4. Consider uncertainty and safeguards: Identify knowledge gaps and measures capable of reducing risk.
  5. Support a decision and review: Decide whether the activity may proceed, whether additional information is necessary, and whether monitoring or restrictions are appropriate.

Environmental risk assessment of genetically modified crops

Genetically modified crops may be developed for useful characteristics such as resistance to particular insect pests, improved nutritional quality or tolerance to certain environmental stresses. However, the intended benefit must be examined alongside possible unintended effects.

Effects on non-target organisms

A crop designed to affect a particular insect pest may require assessment of possible effects on organisms that are not intended targets. These can include beneficial insects and other components of the local ecosystem.

An observed effect must be interpreted in relation to realistic exposure, the biological characteristic being studied and an appropriate comparison crop.

Gene flow

Gene flow is the movement of genetic material between populations. In flowering plants, it may occur through pollen movement and reproduction with compatible plants.

For a genetically modified crop, assessors may examine whether an introduced characteristic could move into compatible cultivated or wild relatives and whether that movement could have harmful consequences.

Gene flow is not automatically harmful. Its significance depends on the characteristic transferred, the receiving population and the environmental conditions.

Effects on agricultural practices

Risk assessment may consider whether cultivation could encourage changes such as the development of resistance in target pests. This is important because a useful agricultural trait may become less effective over time if resistance develops.

Food and feed considerations

Where relevant, safety evaluation may also examine possible toxicity, allergenicity and changes in nutritional composition. An introduced gene does not by itself prove that a food is harmful; equally, an intended agricultural advantage does not establish that every possible food-safety concern has been resolved.

Risk assessment and risk management

Risk assessment identifies and evaluates possible harm. Risk management selects measures to prevent or reduce unacceptable risks.

Management decisions may include restrictions on an activity, additional evaluation, appropriate containment, monitoring or refusal of a proposed release. The specific response depends on the evidence and the applicable regulatory requirements.

The Cartagena Protocol requires scientifically sound risk assessment for decisions within its framework. Its Annex III also explains that scientific uncertainty should not automatically be interpreted as proof that risk is absent or acceptable.

Uncertainty is not proof of danger, but it is also not proof of safety. Where evidence is insufficient, further evaluation or proportionate precaution may be necessary.

Application: evaluating an insect-resistant crop

Suppose a genetically engineered cotton variety is designed to resist a particular insect pest. Its intended benefit is protection against that pest. An environmental assessment would distinguish this expected effect from separate questions about non-target organisms, possible gene flow and effects on agricultural ecosystems.

The relevant question is not whether all genetically modified crops are safe or unsafe. It is whether the particular organism, characteristic, intended use and receiving environment present acceptable risks under the proposed conditions.

Prelims focus

  • A hazard is a potential source of harm; risk depends on exposure, likelihood and consequences.
  • Environmental assessment of a modified crop can include non-target effects, gene flow and ecological consequences.
  • The Cartagena Protocol addresses biosafety risks of living modified organisms.
  • Annex III of the Cartagena Protocol deals with risk assessment.
  • Trap: Gene flow is a biological process, not an automatic finding of environmental damage.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class XII, Chapter 12, Biotechnology and its Applications, Sections 12.1 and 12.4, pp. 207–214; Convention on Biological Diversity, Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, Article 15 and Annex III, Risk Assessment; World Health Organization, Laboratory Biosafety Manual, 4th edition, 2020, Risk Assessment monograph, Overview. Online sources consulted 13 November 2026.]
